page: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard4.Ax.Flex.32-128 is a compute-focused virtual machine instance built on the x86_64 architecture. Powered by the Intel Xeon 6987C-P processor running at 3.9 GHz, the server provides 32 dedicated physical cores and 64 virtual central processing units via two threads per core. Memory capacity is configured at 128 GB, establishing a 2 GB per vCPU ratio that prioritizes raw processing density over oversized memory allocations.

The hardware configuration includes one complimentary public IPv4 address and contains no integrated local storage or graphics processing units. Storage requirements must be satisfied through external block volumes, and graphical or machine learning acceleration is unsupported due to the zero-GPU design. The dedicated CPU allocation ensures reliable execution by mitigating noisy-neighbor contention across virtualized environments.

From an infrastructure cost perspective, the instance maximizes resource utilization for compute-heavy systems by avoiding expenditures on unutilized RAM or local NVMe disks. Workloads aligned with this hardware profile include parallel compilation pipelines, distributed computational tasks, batch video transcoding, CI/CD runners, and horizontally scaled microservices.
description: Oracle Cloud Infrastructure VM.Standard4.Ax.Flex.32-128 is an x86_64 compute-oriented virtual machine powered by an Intel Xeon 6987C-P processor operating at 3.9 GHz. It provisions 32 dedicated physical cores yielding 64 vCPUs alongside 128 GB of system memory, maintaining a 2 GB per vCPU compute-optimized footprint. The server includes one public IPv4 address, contains no auxiliary GPUs, and provides no local disk storage, necessitating network-attached block storage for persistent state. By dedicating CPU cores and omitting surplus memory overhead, the instance delivers qualitative cost efficiency for processor-saturated workloads. VM.Standard4.Ax.Flex.32-128 is engineered for batch processing, continuous integration build jobs, video encoding pipelines, and high-concurrency stateless web services.
